summary.text: A martingale is a stochastic process in which the expected value of the next observation, given all prior observations, equals the most recent value.
Martingales model fair games, where future expected winnings equal the current amount regardless of past outcomes.
The word first meant 18th-century French betting strategies, like doubling the bet after each loss, which bankrupt their users because bankrolls are finite.

items.prompt: After five losses in a row in a fair game, a gambler feels a win is due. What does the martingale model say about expected winnings from here?

options.label: They are unchanged by the past losses

items.prompt: A population of fixed size changes only by genetic drift, with no mutation or selection. What does this say about an allele's frequency?

options.label: It is expected to rise every generation
It follows a martingale, so its expected next value is its current value
It is expected to fall every generation
It must stay exactly the same in every generation

items.explain: Under genetic drift alone the allele frequency follows a martingale, meaning its expected next value equals its latest value, though actual values can still change.

items.prompt: Someone claims a process is a martingale. Can it fail to be one when judged with a different probability measure?

options.label: No, being a martingale never depends on the measure
No, but only when it is a random walk
Yes, it can be a martingale for one measure but not another
Yes, but only for continuous-time processes

items.explain: The martingale property involves both the filtration and the probability measure, so a process may be a martingale for one measure and not another.

paragraphs.heading: Your best guess is where you are
paragraphs.text: A martingale is a process that unfolds over time with a particular kind of balance. Suppose you know every value it has taken so far. Then your expected value for the next step is exactly the value you see right now. Put another way, once you condition on the whole past, the expected next value equals the present one.

paragraphs.heading: A model of a fair game
paragraphs.text: Martingales are used to describe fair games. In such a game, what you expect to hold later equals what you hold now, whatever happened in earlier rounds. Picture a gambler who wins $1 when a fair coin lands heads and loses $1 when it lands tails. Given the history so far, the expected fortune after the next toss is just the current fortune. In general, a gambler's capital is a martingale whenever every game they play is fair.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The word first named a family of betting strategies that were popular in France in the 1700s. The simplest was for a coin game: the gambler wins the stake on heads and loses it on tails. After every loss the bet was doubled, so that one win would cancel all earlier losses and leave a profit equal to the first stake. With wealth and time both growing without end, the chance of heads eventually showing up approaches 1, so the plan looks like a sure thing. In practice the bets grow exponentially, and a finite bankroll eventually runs dry.

paragraphs.heading: Who built the theory
paragraphs.text: Paul Lévy brought the idea into probability theory in 1934, though he did not give it a name. Ville supplied the word martingale in 1939 and widened the definition to continuous martingales. Joseph Leo Doob, along with others, did much of the early work. One goal of that work was to show with mathematics that no betting strategy can beat a game of chance.

paragraphs.heading: Walks and urns
paragraphs.text: An unbiased random walk is a martingale, whatever the number of dimensions. Think of a point on a line that, at each tick of the clock, steps left or right with equal chance. Pólya's urn gives another example. You pull out a marble at random, then return it together with several more marbles of that same colour. For any one colour, the fraction of the urn it makes up is a martingale.

paragraphs.heading: Estimates that keep updating
paragraphs.text: Martingales also describe learning. Say you want to know some uncertain quantity Y, and information about it arrives bit by bit. If at each stage you take your best estimate of Y given what you know, the sequence of estimates is a martingale. Stopped Brownian motion, itself a martingale, can likewise trace out how a fair game unfolds.
